blocks.section: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

blocks.text: Abstract
blocks.raw_text: Abstract

blocks.text: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT , which stands for B idirectional E ncoder R epresentations from T ransformers. Unlike recent language representation models (Peters et al., 2018a; Radford et al., 2018), BERT is designed to pretrain deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be finetuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial taskspecific architecture modifications.

blocks.text: BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (7.7% point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).

blocks.text: 1 Introduction
blocks.raw_text: 1 Introduction

blocks.text: Language model pre-training has been shown to be effective for improving many natural language processing tasks (Dai and Le, 2015; Peters et al., 2018a; Radford et al., 2018; Howard and Ruder, 2018). These include sentence-level tasks such as natural language inference (Bowman et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2018) and paraphrasing (Dolan and Brockett, 2005), which aim to predict the relationships between sentences by analyzing them holistically, as well as token-level tasks such as named entity recognition and question answering, where models are required to produce fine-grained output at the token level (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003; Rajpurkar et al., 2016).
blocks.raw_text: Language model pre-training has been shown to be effective for improving many natural language processing tasks (Dai and Le, 2015; Peters et al., 2018a; Radford et al., 2018; Howard and Ruder, 2018). These include sentence-level tasks such as natural language inference (Bowman et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2018) and paraphrasing (Dolan and Brockett, 2005), which aim to predict the relationships between sentences by analyzing them holistically, as well as token-level tasks such as named entity recognition and question answering, where models are required to produce fine-grained output at the token level (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003; Rajpurkar et al., 2016).

blocks.text: There are two existing strategies for applying pre-trained language representations to downstream tasks: feature-based and fi ne-tuning . The feature-based approach, such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018a), uses task-specific architectures that include the pre-trained representations as additional features. The fine-tuning approach, such as the Generative Pre-trained Transformer (OpenAI GPT) (Radford et al., 2018), introduces minimal task-specific parameters, and is trained on the downstream tasks by simply fine-tuning all pretrained parameters. The two approaches share the same objective function during pre-training, where they use unidirectional language models to learn general language representations.

blocks.text: We argue that current techniques restrict the power of the pre-trained representations, especially for the fine-tuning approaches. The major limitation is that standard language models are unidirectional, and this limits the choice of architectures that can be used during pre-training. For example, in OpenAI GPT, the authors use a left-toright architecture, where every token can only attend to previous tokens in the self-attention layers of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017). Such restrictions are sub-optimal for sentence-level tasks, and could be very harmful when applying finetuning based approaches to token-level tasks such as question answering, where it is crucial to incorporate context from both directions.

blocks.text: 2.1 Unsupervised Feature-based Approaches
blocks.raw_text: 2.1 Unsupervised Feature-based Approaches

blocks.text: Learning widely applicable representations of words has been an active area of research for decades, including non-neural (Brown et al., 1992; Ando and Zhang, 2005; Blitzer et al., 2006) and neural (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) methods. Pre-trained word embeddings are an integral part of modern NLP systems, offering significant improvements over embeddings learned from scratch (Turian et al., 2010). To pretrain word embedding vectors, left-to-right language modeling objectives have been used (Mnih and Hinton, 2009), as well as objectives to discriminate correct from incorrect words in left and right context (Mikolov et al., 2013).

blocks.text: These approaches have been generalized to coarser granularities, such as sentence embeddings (Kiros et al., 2015; Logeswaran and Lee, 2018) or paragraph embeddings (Le and Mikolov, 2014). To train sentence representations, prior work has used objectives to rank candidate next sentences (Jernite et al., 2017; Logeswaran and Lee, 2018), left-to-right generation of next sentence words given a representation of the previous sentence (Kiros et al., 2015), or denoising autoencoder derived objectives (Hill et al., 2016).

blocks.text: ELMo and its predecessor (Peters et al., 2017, 2018a) generalize traditional word embedding research along a different dimension. They extract context-sensitive features from a left-to-right and a right-to-left language model. The contextual representation of each token is the concatenation of the left-to-right and right-to-left representations. When integrating contextual word embeddings with existing task-specific architectures, ELMo advances the state of the art for several major NLP benchmarks (Peters et al., 2018a) including question answering (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), sentiment analysis (Socher et al., 2013), and named entity recognition (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003). Melamud et al. (2016) proposed learning contextual representations through a task to predict a single word from both left and right context using LSTMs. Similar to ELMo, their model is feature-based and not deeply bidirectional. Fedus et al. (2018) shows that the cloze task can be used to improve the robustness of text generation models.

blocks.raw_text: 3 BERT

blocks.text: We introduce BERT and its detailed implementation in this section. There are two steps in our framework: pre-training and fi ne-tuning . During pre-training, the model is trained on unlabeled data over different pre-training tasks. For finetuning, the BERT model is first initialized with the pre-trained parameters, and all of the parameters are fine-tuned using labeled data from the downstream tasks. Each downstream task has separate fine-tuned models, even though they are initialized with the same pre-trained parameters. The question-answering example in Figure 1 will serve as a running example for this section.

blocks.text: Input/Output Representations To make BERT handle a variety of down-stream tasks, our input representation is able to unambiguously represent both a single sentence and a pair of sentences (e.g., 〈 Question, Answer 〉 ) in one token sequence. Throughout this work, a 'sentence' can be an arbitrary span of contiguous text, rather than an actual linguistic sentence. A 'sequence' refers to the input token sequence to BERT, which may be a single sentence or two sentences packed together.

blocks.text: Task #1: Masked LM Intuitively, it is reasonable to believe that a deep bidirectional model is strictly more powerful than either a left-to-right model or the shallow concatenation of a left-toright and a right-to-left model. Unfortunately, standard conditional language models can only be trained left-to-right or right-to-left, since bidirectional conditioning would allow each word to indirectly 'see itself', and the model could trivially predict the target word in a multi-layered context.

blocks.text: In order to train a deep bidirectional representation, we simply mask some percentage of the input tokens at random, and then predict those masked tokens. We refer to this procedure as a 'masked LM' (MLM), although it is often referred to as a Cloze task in the literature (Taylor, 1953). In this case, the final hidden vectors corresponding to the mask tokens are fed into an output softmax over the vocabulary, as in a standard LM. In all of our experiments, we mask 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence at random. In contrast to denoising auto-encoders (Vincent et al., 2008), we only predict the masked words rather than reconstructing the entire input.

blocks.text: Task #2: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) Many important downstream tasks such as Question Answering (QA) and Natural Language Inference (NLI) are based on understanding the relationship between two sentences, which is not directly captured by language modeling. In order to train a model that understands sentence relationships, we pre-train for a binarized next sentence prediction task that can be trivially generated from any monolingual corpus. Specifically, when choosing the sentences A and B for each pretraining example, 50% of the time B is the actual next sentence that follows A (labeled as IsNext ), and 50% of the time it is a random sentence from the corpus (labeled as NotNext ). As we show in Figure 1, C is used for next sentence prediction (NSP). 5 Despite its simplicity, we demonstrate in Section 5.1 that pre-training towards this task is very beneficial to both QA and NLI. 6

blocks.text: Fine-tuning is straightforward since the selfattention mechanism in the Transformer allows BERT to model many downstream taskswhether they involve single text or text pairs-by swapping out the appropriate inputs and outputs. For applications involving text pairs, a common pattern is to independently encode text pairs before applying bidirectional cross attention, such as Parikh et al. (2016); Seo et al. (2017). BERT instead uses the self-attention mechanism to unify these two stages, as encoding a concatenated text pair with self-attention effectively includes bidirectional cross attention between two sentences.

blocks.text: As shown in Figure 1, in the question answering task, we represent the input question and passage as a single packed sequence, with the question using the A embedding and the passage using the B embedding. We only introduce a start vector S ∈ R H and an end vector E ∈ R H during fine-tuning. The probability of word i being the start of the answer span is computed as a dot product between T i and S followed by a softmax over all of the words in the paragraph: P i = e S · T i ∑ j e S · T j . The analogous formula is used for the end of the answer span. The score of a candidate span from position i to position j is defined as S · T i + E · T j , and the maximum scoring span where j ≥ i is used as a prediction. The training objective is the sum of the log-likelihoods of the correct start and end positions. We fine-tune for 3 epochs with a learning rate of 5e-5 and a batch size of 32.

blocks.text: 5.3 Feature-based Approach with BERT
blocks.raw_text: 5.3 Feature-based Approach with BERT

blocks.text: All of the BERT results presented so far have used the fine-tuning approach, where a simple classification layer is added to the pre-trained model, and all parameters are jointly fine-tuned on a downstream task. However, the feature-based approach, where fixed features are extracted from the pretrained model, has certain advantages. First, not all tasks can be easily represented by a Transformer encoder architecture, and therefore require a task-specific model architecture to be added. Second, there are major computational benefits to pre-compute an expensive representation of the training data once and then run many experiments with cheaper models on top of this representation.

blocks.text: 6 Conclusion
blocks.raw_text: 6 Conclusion

blocks.text: Recent empirical improvements due to transfer learning with language models have demonstrated that rich, unsupervised pre-training is an integral part of many language understanding systems. In particular, these results enable even low-resource tasks to benefit from deep unidirectional architectures. Our major contribution is further generalizing these findings to deep bidirectional architectures, allowing the same pre-trained model to successfully tackle a broad set of NLP tasks.

blocks.text: To generate each training input sequence, we sample two spans of text from the corpus, which we refer to as 'sentences' even though they are typically much longer than single sentences (but can be shorter also). They are sampled such that the combined length is ≤ 512 tokens. The LM masking is applied after WordPiece tokenization with a uniform masking rate of 15%, and no special consideration given to partial word pieces.

blocks.section: A.4 Comparison of BERT, ELMo ,and OpenAI GPT

analysis.title: BERT：深度双向Transformer预训练论文阅读看板
analysis.summary: 论文提出BERT，一种通过深度双向Transformer从无标签文本预训练语言表示的模型。它使用掩码语言模型和下一句预测两个无监督任务，在GLUE、SQuAD和SWAG等11个NLP任务上取得当时最优结果。看板从研究问题、预训练方法、微调策略、实验证据、消融分析和贡献局限六个方面组织。
analysis.research_question: 如何通过深度双向预训练获得通用语言表示，使同一模型微调后能处理多种自然语言处理任务？
reading_guide: 先阅读引言和结论，理解BERT要解决的单向语言模型局限和双向预训练目标。
进入方法部分，关注MLM和NSP两个预训练任务、输入表示以及模型尺寸配置。
查看GLUE、SQuAD v1.1/v2.0和SWAG实验表格，注意具体指标、对比基线和提升数值。
阅读消融研究，理解预训练任务、模型规模、掩码策略和特征方法对性能的贡献。
最后阅读附录和局限说明，了解WNLI排除、RTE多任务未报告等适用边界。

nodes.title: BERT：深度双向Transformer预训练
nodes.summary: 论文提出BERT，一种通过深度双向Transformer从无标签文本预训练语言表示的模型；它联合条件化左右上下文，并可通过一个额外输出层微调。摘要报告在11个NLP任务上取得新的最优结果，其中GLUE分数80.5%（绝对提升7.7点）、MultiNLI准确率86.7%（绝对提升4.6点）。
nodes.explanation: BERT的核心是使用掩码语言模型和下一句预测两个无监督任务预训练深度双向表示，区别于当时使用单向语言模型的预训练方法。

nodes.title: 研究问题与动机
nodes.summary: 论文研究如何通过深度双向预训练获得通用语言表示，使同一模型微调后能处理多种NLP任务。此前单向语言模型（如GPT）只能利用左侧上下文，限制了对双向语境的理解。
nodes.explanation: 研究问题聚焦于预训练目标与架构的双向性，而非特定任务架构设计。

nodes.title: 预训练方法
nodes.summary: BERT使用多层双向Transformer编码器，通过掩码语言模型（MLM）和下一句预测（NSP）两个无监督任务预训练。MLM随机遮盖输入token并预测，NSP判断句子对是否连续。
nodes.explanation: 预训练方法决定了模型学习到的表示质量，双向性和两个任务的联合训练是核心设计。

nodes.title: 模型架构与输入表示
nodes.summary: BERT采用多层双向Transformer编码器；报告BERTBASE（L=12, H=768, A=12, 110M参数）和BERTLARGE（L=24, H=1024, A=16, 340M参数）。输入用30,000词WordPiece嵌入，[CLS]最终隐藏状态作为分类聚合表示，句子对用[SEP]分隔并为句子A/B添加学习嵌入。
nodes.explanation: BASE与LARGE是不同容量的两种配置；输入表示由token、segment和position嵌入相加构成，[CLS]与[SEP]使单句和句对能在同一序列中处理。

nodes.title: 预训练任务：MLM与NSP
nodes.summary: MLM随机选择15%的WordPiece token进行预测，其中80%替换为[MASK]，10%替换为随机token，10%保持不变，以缓解预训练与微调的不匹配。NSP中50%的句子对为连续下一句（IsNext），50%为随机句子（NotNext）。
nodes.explanation: MLM类似完形填空，迫使模型利用双向上下文；NSP让模型学习句子间关系，用于问答和推理等任务。

nodes.title: 掩码策略与预训练数据
nodes.summary: 预训练数据为BooksCorpus（800M词）和英文维基百科（2,500M词），使用文档级语料以抽取长连续序列；掩码语言模型在WordPiece后以15%均匀率掩码。批量256个序列（128,000 token/批），训练1,000,000步，约40个epoch（3.3B词语料）；Adam学习率1e-4，前10,000步预热后线性衰减。
nodes.explanation: 文档级语料而非打乱句级语料有助于抽取长连续输入；15%均匀掩码是MLM的预训练策略。大批量、长步数与预热后线性衰减是预训练优化设置。

nodes.title: 微调策略
nodes.summary: BERT微调把任务特定的输入输出接入预训练模型，并端到端微调全部参数；微调相对经济，论文中所有结果可在单块Cloud TPU上最多1小时、或在GPU上数小时内复现，起点是同一个预训练模型。多数下游任务只需增加额外输出层，无需大幅修改任务特定架构。
nodes.explanation: Transformer自注意力使BERT能用同一架构处理单文本或文本对任务，只需替换相应输入输出；新增输出层即可适配广泛任务。

nodes.title: GLUE微调细节
nodes.summary: GLUE微调使用批量大小32、训练3个epoch；每个任务在开发集从5e-5、4e-5、3e-5、2e-5中选择最佳学习率。BERTLARGE在小数据集上有时不稳定，因此用相同预训练检查点做多次随机重启，仅改变微调数据打乱和分类层初始化，并按开发集选最佳模型。分类使用[CLS]最终隐藏向量C∈R^H作为聚合表示，新增分类层权重W∈R^{K×H}，以log(softmax(CW^T))计算分类损失。
nodes.explanation: 随机重启指复用同一预训练检查点，改变下游微调的数据顺序和分类层初始化；[CLS]向量C作为整段输入的聚合表示，分类层只新增W。

nodes.title: SQuAD与SWAG微调设置
nodes.summary: SQuAD v1.1把问题/段落打包为单序列，仅新增起止向量S和E，训练目标为正确起止位置对数似然之和；微调3个epoch、学习率5e-5、批大小32。SQuAD 2.0把无答案视为起止都在[CLS]的跨度，比较无答案得分s_null与最佳非空跨度，开发集选择阈值τ；微调2个epoch、学习率5e-5、批大小48。SWAG为四个候选续写分别构造输入序列，仅新增与[CLS]表示C点积的打分向量，经softmax归一化；微调3个epoch、学习率2e-5、批大小16。
nodes.explanation: 起止向量把问答建模为在段落中选一个连续跨度；SQuAD 2.0把无答案也纳入同一打分空间，阈值τ在开发集上选择；SWAG对四个候选续写分别打分并用softmax归一化。

nodes.title: 11项NLP任务上的实验证据
nodes.summary: BERT在11项自然语言处理任务上取得当时最优结果。摘要报告GLUE得分80.5（绝对提升7.7个百分点）、MultiNLI准确率86.7（绝对提升4.6个百分点）、SQuAD v1.1测试F1 93.2（绝对提升1.5点）和SQuAD v2.0测试F1 83.1（绝对提升5.1点）；实验部分还包含SWAG等任务。这些结果支持深度双向预训练在下游任务上的有效性。
nodes.explanation: GLUE、MultiNLI、SQuAD和SWAG分别覆盖句子级理解、自然语言推断、问答与常识推理；绝对提升指准确率或F1提高的百分点，而非相对百分比。

nodes.title: GLUE与SQuAD v1.1结果
nodes.summary: GLUE测试集上，BERTBASE和BERTLARGE平均准确率分别比此前最优提升4.5和7.0个百分点；BERTLARGE官方GLUE得分80.5，OpenAI GPT为72.8。MNLI绝对准确率提升4.6个百分点。SQuAD v1.1上，BERTLARGE单模型开发集F1 90.9，7模型集成开发集91.8；经TriviaQA微调后单模型测试F1 91.8，集成测试F1 93.2，比当时排行榜最佳集成高1.5 F1。
nodes.explanation: 原文用百分号符号表达绝对准确率提升，换算为百分点更准确；SQuAD数值为F1，且区分单模型/集成以及开发集/测试集。

nodes.title: SQuAD v2.0与SWAG结果
nodes.summary: SQuAD 2.0上，BERT LARGE单模型开发集EM 78.7、F1 81.9，测试集EM 80.0、F1 83.1，相对此前最佳系统提升+5.1 F1。SWAG上，BERT LARGE开发集86.6、测试集86.3，比ESIM+ELMo高+27.1%，比OpenAI GPT高8.3%。
nodes.explanation: SQuAD 2.0包含无答案问题，提升5.1 F1；SWAG准确率对比中，ESIM+ELMo测试集为59.2，差距明显。

nodes.title: 消融与机制分析
nodes.summary: BERT通过消融比较预训练任务、模型规模、掩码策略及特征式与微调方法：移除NSP会损害QNLI、MNLI和SQuAD 1.1；LTR模型在所有任务上弱于MLM；更大模型在所选GLUE任务上带来严格精度提升；拼接最后4层仅比全模型微调低0.3 F1。
nodes.explanation: 消融实验用于分离各设计选择对下游性能的贡献，而不仅是报告最终分数；双向MLM/NSP、模型规模、掩码分布和是否微调都被分别检验。

nodes.title: 预训练任务与模型规模消融
nodes.summary: 移除NSP在QNLI、MNLI和SQuAD 1.1上显著损害性能；LTR模型在所有任务上弱于MLM，添加BiLSTM仍远差于双向预训练。模型规模消融显示，更大模型在四个数据集上均严格提升准确率，即使MRPC仅3,600样本。
nodes.explanation: 消融表明NSP和双向性都是关键；规模增大对下游任务有稳定增益。

nodes.title: 掩码策略与特征方法消融
nodes.summary: 在MNLI开发集微调与CoNLL-2003 NER上，不同MASK/SAME/RND掩码比例对微调结果影响较小；特征式NER中仅用MASK或仅用RND时表现较差。特征式方法拼接最后4层仅比全模型微调低0.3 F1。
nodes.explanation: 微调能调整表示以适应任务，因此对预训练掩码策略不敏感；特征式方法固定表示，掩码分布不匹配时NER更易受影响。

nodes.title: 贡献与结论
nodes.summary: 论文的主要贡献是把已有关于深度单向架构的发现进一步推广到深度双向架构，使同一预训练模型能处理广泛NLP任务。结论强调丰富的无监督预训练是许多语言理解系统的重要组成部分。
nodes.explanation: 贡献在于证明深度双向预训练能作为通用语言表示，支持多类NLP任务，而非只提升单一基准。

nodes.title: 主要贡献：推广深度双向预训练架构
nodes.summary: 相对于使用单向语言模型的OpenAI GPT等预训练方法，BERT通过掩码语言模型（MLM）实现深度双向表示，并联合使用下一句预测（NSP）预训练文本对表示。消融实验显示，移除NSP会显著降低QNLI、MNLI和SQuAD 1.1性能；改用从左到右（LTR）模型也在所有任务上更差，MRPC和SQuAD下降明显。
nodes.explanation: 核心证据是Table 5的消融：去NSP在QNLI、MNLI、SQuAD等下降，LTR & No NSP在MRPC、SQuAD下降更大，说明双向性和NSP对下游性能有贡献。

nodes.title: 局限与边界：WNLI排除、RTE单任务与MLM效率
nodes.summary: GLUE的WNLI因数据集构建问题且所有已提交系统低于多数类基线65.1%被排除；正文只报告单任务微调，作者提示多任务微调可能进一步提升，并称在RTE上用MNLI多任务训练观察到显著改进。预训练方面，MLM每批只对15% token做预测，可能需要更多步数，且收敛略慢于从左到右模型，但论文称经验提升远超过增加的训练成本。
nodes.explanation: 这些边界限定结论范围：WNLI不适合纳入平均分，RTE结果可能因仅单任务而保守，MLM的预测稀疏和收敛较慢是效率代价。

nodes.title: WNLI因构建问题被排除
nodes.summary: GLUE网页指出WNLI数据集存在构建问题，且所有已提交GLUE的训练系统都低于预测多数类的65.1%准确率基线。因此，论文为公平比较排除WNLI；BERT在GLUE提交中对WNLI始终预测多数类。
nodes.explanation: 排除是为公平比较；Table 1平均分也因排除WNLI而略异于官方GLUE分数，BERT提交时对WNLI始终预测多数类。

nodes.title: RTE多任务微调未报告
nodes.summary: 作者仅报告RTE单任务微调结果，并指出多任务微调可能进一步提升性能，例如从MNLI多任务训练中观察到RTE有显著改进。
nodes.explanation: 这意味着本文的RTE结果可能低于通过多任务学习可达到的水平，但作者未在本文中系统研究。

nodes.title: MLM预训练成本与收敛速度
nodes.summary: 与从左到右语言模型相比，MLM每批只对15%的token做预测，因此可能需要更多预训练步数；原文称其收敛仅略慢，且经验改进远超增加的训练成本。预训练成本还体现在硬件规模：BERTBASE使用16个TPU芯片，BERTLARGE使用64个TPU芯片，两者各训练4天。
nodes.explanation: MLM并非对每个token都计算预测损失，而是随机掩码15%的WordPiece token并只预测这些位置；因此每批提供的预测信号少于从左到右模型，可能需要更多步收敛。原文认为这种效率代价换来双向表示收益，且成本增加可接受。

evidence.quote: BERT is designed to pretrain deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers.
BERT alleviates the previously mentioned unidirectionality constraint by using a 'masked language model' (MLM) pre-training objective
we also use a 'next sentence prediction' task that jointly pretrains text-pair representations.
We primarily report results on two model sizes: BERTBASE (L=12, H=768, A=12, Total Parameters=110M) and BERTLARGE (L=24, H=1024, A=16, Total Parameters=340M).

BERTBASE was chosen to have the same model size as OpenAI GPT for comparison purposes. Critically, however, the BERT Transformer uses bidirectional self-attention, while the GPT Transformer uses constrained self-attention where every token can only attend to context to its left.
our input representation is able to unambiguously represent both a single sentence and a pair of sentences (e.g., 〈 Question, Answer 〉 ) in one token sequence.
We use WordPiece embeddings (Wu et al., 2016) with a 30,000 token vocabulary. The first token of every sequence is always a special classification token ( [CLS] ).

It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (7.7% point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).

Unlike Peters et al. (2018a) and Radford et al. (2018), we do not use traditional left-to-right or right-to-left language models to pre-train BERT. Instead, we pre-train BERT using two unsupervised tasks, described in this section.
In all of our experiments, we mask 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence at random.

The training data generator chooses 15% of the token positions at random for prediction. If the i -th token is chosen, we replace the i -th token with (1) the [MASK] token 80% of the time (2) a random token 10% of the time (3) the unchanged i -th token 10% of the time.

Specifically, when choosing the sentences A and B for each pretraining example, 50% of the time B is the actual next sentence that follows A (labeled as IsNext ), and 50% of the time it is a random sentence from the corpus (labeled as NotNext ).

For the pre-training corpus we use the BooksCorpus (800M words) (Zhu et al., 2015) and English Wikipedia (2,500M words). For Wikipedia we extract only the text passages and ignore lists, tables, and headers. It is critical to use a document-level corpus rather than a shuffled sentence-level corpus such as the Billion Word Benchmark (Chelba et al., 2013) in order to extract long contiguous sequences.
For each task, we simply plug in the taskspecific inputs and outputs into BERT and finetune all the parameters end-to-end.

Compared to pre-training, fine-tuning is relatively inexpensive. All of the results in the paper can be replicated in at most 1 hour on a single Cloud TPU, or a few hours on a GPU, starting from the exact same pre-trained model.
We use a batch size of 32 and fine-tune for 3 epochs over the data for all GLUE tasks. For each task, we selected the best fine-tuning learning rate (among 5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5, and 2e-5) on the Dev set.
Both BERTBASE and BERTLARGE outperform all systems on all tasks by a substantial margin, obtaining 4.5% and 7.0% respective average accuracy improvement over the prior state of the art.
For the largest and most widely reported GLUE task, MNLI, BERT obtains a 4.6% absolute accuracy improvement.
On the official GLUEleaderboard 10 , BERTLARGE obtains a score of 80.5, compared to OpenAI GPT, which obtains 72.8 as of the date of writing.

Our best performing system outperforms the top leaderboard system by +1.5 F1 in ensembling and +1.3 F1 as a single system. In fact, our single BERT model outperforms the top ensemble system in terms of F1 score.
BERT LARGE (Single) | 84.1 | 90.9 | - | - |
BERT LARGE (Ens.+TriviaQA) | 86.2 | 92.2 | 87.4 | 93.2 |

To fine-tune on GLUE, we represent the input sequence (for single sentence or sentence pairs) as described in Section 3, and use the final hidden vector C ∈ R H corresponding to the first input token ( [CLS] ) as the aggregate representation. The only new parameters introduced during fine-tuning are classification layer weights W ∈ R K × H , where K is the number of labels.

As shown in Figure 1, in the question answering task, we represent the input question and passage as a single packed sequence, with the question using the A embedding and the passage using the B embedding. We only introduce a start vector S ∈ R H and an end vector E ∈ R H during fine-tuning.
The training objective is the sum of the log-likelihoods of the correct start and end positions. We fine-tune for 3 epochs with a learning rate of 5e-5 and a batch size of 32.

Weuse a simple approach to extend the SQuAD v1.1 BERT model for this task. We treat questions that do not have an answer as having an answer span with start and end at the [CLS] token. The probability space for the start and end answer span positions is extended to include the position of the [CLS] token.

We predict a non-null answer when ˆ s i,j > s null + τ , where the threshold τ is selected on the dev set to maximize F1. We did not use TriviaQA data for this model. We fine-tuned for 2 epochs with a learning rate of 5e-5 and a batch size of 48.

The results compared to prior leaderboard entries and top published work (Sun et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018b) are shown in Table 3, excluding systems that use BERT as one of their components. We observe a +5.1 F1 improvement over the previous best system.
| BERT LARGE (Single) | Ours | 78.7 | 81.9 | 80.0 | 83.1 |

The Situations With Adversarial Generations (SWAG) dataset contains 113k sentence-pair completion examples that evaluate grounded commonsense inference (Zellers et al., 2018). Given a sentence, the task is to choose the most plausible continuation among four choices.

When fine-tuning on the SWAG dataset, we construct four input sequences, each containing the concatenation of the given sentence (sentence A ) and a possible continuation (sentence B ). The only task-specific parameters introduced is a vector whose dot product with the [CLS] token representation C denotes a score for each choice which is normalized with a softmax layer.

We fine-tune the model for 3 epochs with a learning rate of 2e-5 and a batch size of 16. Results are presented in Table 4. BERTLARGE outperforms the authors' baseline ESIM+ELMo system by +27.1% and OpenAI GPT by 8.3%.

Wefirst examine the impact brought by the NSP task. In Table 5, we show that removing NSP hurts performance significantly on QNLI, MNLI, and SQuAD 1.1. Next, we evaluate the impact of training bidirectional representations by comparing 'No NSP' to 'LTR & No NSP'. The LTR model performs worse than the MLM model on all tasks, with large drops on MRPC and SQuAD.

Results on selected GLUE tasks are shown in Table 6. In this table, we report the average Dev Set accuracy from 5 random restarts of fine-tuning. We can see that larger models lead to a strict accuracy improvement across all four datasets, even for MRPC which only has 3,600 labeled training examples, and is substantially different from the pre-training tasks. It is also perhaps surprising that we are able to achieve such significant improvements on top of models which are already quite large relative to the existing literature.
BERTBASE contains 110M parameters and BERTLARGE contains 340M parameters.

To ablate the fine-tuning approach, we apply the feature-based approach by extracting the activations from one or more layers without fi ne-tuning any parameters of BERT. These contextual embeddings are used as input to a randomly initialized two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM before the classification layer.

Results are presented in Table 7. BERTLARGE performs competitively with state-of-the-art methods. The best performing method concatenates the token representations from the top four hidden layers of the pre-trained Transformer, which is only 0.3 F1 behind fine-tuning the entire model. This demonstrates that BERT is effective for both finetuning and feature-based approaches.
The SQuAD 2.0 task extends the SQuAD 1.1 problem definition by allowing for the possibility that no short answer exists in the provided paragraph, making the problem more realistic.

However, the feature-based approach, where fixed features are extracted from the pretrained model, has certain advantages. First, not all tasks can be easily represented by a Transformer encoder architecture, and therefore require a task-specific model architecture to be added. Second, there are major computational benefits to pre-compute an expensive representation of the training data once and then run many experiments with cheaper models on top of this representation.
Our major contribution is further generalizing these findings to deep bidirectional architectures, allowing the same pre-trained model to successfully tackle a broad set of NLP tasks.

Recent empirical improvements due to transfer learning with language models have demonstrated that rich, unsupervised pre-training is an integral part of many language understanding systems. In particular, these results enable even low-resource tasks to benefit from deep unidirectional architectures. Our major contribution is further generalizing these findings to deep bidirectional architectures, allowing the same pre-trained model to successfully tackle a broad set of NLP tasks.
Unlike Radford et al. (2018), which uses unidirectional language models for pre-training, BERT uses masked language models to enable pretrained deep bidirectional representations.
